utterances.text: [In English] "Q. What specific role did you have once the police stations had been set up in relation to those police stations? "A. I wanted the people working for the police to do their work properly and fairly irrespective of the ethnic background of anyone, including those who had violated the law and who acted well beyond what would one would consider normal in such circumstances. "Q. Were you then in charge of these police stations? "A. Yes, I was, but they all had their own respective station commanders. At the ministry, I also had a number of associates assisting me in doing everything properly. "Q. On a day-to-day level were you making the operative operational decisions about how the police stations or how the commanders of the police station should work? "A. Yes, together with my staff at the ministry we worked on that. I had people who had worked for the police for a number of years and who were familiar with many tasks. "Q. Were you attempting to protect only Serbians, or were you trying to protect civilians in general? "A. As I have said a moment ago, it was our duty and obligation to protect all citizens living there, those who behaved properly, who did not do anything wrong and lived normally. "Q. Were you personally in daily or weekly contact with Hadzic at this time? "A. Yes, I was. Perhaps not daily but at least weekly." [Interpretation] You remember that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] "What was his attitude towards the work you were doing? "A. He never said that something was wrong. He seemed content with what I was doing at least as far as I know. "Q. Looking at paragraph 14, Mr. Bogunovic, and the first statement there, the first sentence states: 'After other areas were freed, there was a need for new stations to be set point up ...' Then there is's a whole list of stations. What did you mean when you said 'after other areas were freed?' Why did you use the word 'freed?' "A. I used the word 'freed' because there were parts of that region which were inaccessible to us. There were barricades, and no movement was possible for civilians and Serbian civilians in particular to move about those parties. "Q. Are you able to pin-point with any accuracy when it was that the villages in the SBWS were freed, as you describe it? Was there a point in time when the government agreed that the villages had been freed? "A. On the 20th of September, we began liberating such locations, and Vukovar was freed sometime in November, around 20th of November. That's the period in question. "Q. And so by November or late November, early December, all the villages had been freed? "A. Yes, as well as Vukovar. "Q. When did the JNA leave the region? "A. The JNA left the region, as far as I recall, towards the end of 1991 or the beginning of 1992. "Q. And until they left the region, they were in effective command of the freeing of villages; is that correct? "A. Yes. "Q. Would you have a look at paragraph 23 of your statement, P553, please. 'We didn't notice the presence of the MUP of Serbia in the take-over of the villages. Everything was led by the army.' Would you agree with me, then, what you saw and what you observed was the JNA and not the MUP of Serbia involved in freeing the villages? "A. Yes, the military and the Territorial Defence together were liberating the villages. The military administration ruled over the entire area up to the 23rd of December, as far as I can remember. "Q. The remainder of the paragraph, paragraph 23, states: "'Apart from Badza, Zavisic, and perhaps one or two other men, we didn't notice anyone else from MUP there.' "Would you agree with me that up until -- "A. Yes, correct. "Q. Would you agree with me that when Badza arrived, he -- no, let me strike that. When did Badza arrive in the SBWS region, can you remember? "A. As far as I can remember, it was a long time ago. That was sometime around mid-August or perhaps even towards the end of August. Possibly even the beginning of September, but I can't remember. "Q. Was this around the time you were setting up the police stations? "A. Yes. "Q. Did Badza come with members of a special unit from the public security of Serbia? "A. No." [Interpretation] You remember these answers of yours? [In English] "Q. Where did he come from, as far as you understand it? "A. As far as I could understand, he had arrived from Belgrade. "Q. Belgrade is a big place. What do you do you mean he came from Belgrade? "A. Well, I mean from the MUP of Serbia. "Q. From what you observed when he arrived, did he assist with providing support to the setting up of the police stations? "A. Well, he did assist, and he told us what we should do to be safe, for all the civilians to be safe or, rather, for all the residents of the area to the safe. "Q. So he moved around the police stations providing that expert advice? "A. Yes. He did move around the police stations that had been set up. He did have experience, and he was in a position to assist us. He was in a position to tell us what to do and how to best go about our business. "Q. Putting aside -- and I'll come to this later, but putting aside his, from what you've described, somewhat overbearing attitude towards you and others, was he engaged in providing security to civilians in the SBWS region in the month after he arrived? "A. By providing us with instructions and advice and so on and so forth, one could notice that he wanted to avoid problems in the liberated areas where the police stations had already been set up. He wanted things to be done in accordance with the law, in accordance to how he saw things should be done." [Interpretation] Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will read out to you another much smaller passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 6041.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You are again questioned by the Defence counsel of Jovica Stanisic. "Could we turn now, please, to paragraph 26 of this statement. Page 6 of the English, and 6 of the B/C/S. "Q. 'I met Jovica Stanisic several times. I had no personal contact with him. He never told me anything about what his role was.' "Is it right that you did not during these events speak to Mr. Stanisic? "A. I don't recall speaking with him. I don't recall any conversations with him. I don't think there were any. "Q. And he never told you anything about what his role was and is it correct that no one else told you what his role was either? "A. At some point in time, Goran told me that Jovica was from the state security but nothing other than that. He didn't specify whether he was a chief. He just said that he was from the DB and that was it. "Q. And from that you understood what? "A. Well, we met other people at the time as well. We wanted to meet anyone who could assist us, provide advice or instructions about what to do. We wanted to meet people who could provide us with what we needed the most at the time, be it financially or in other ways. In any case, that was the reason why we met with people from Serbia. "Q. But you knew Stanisic -- let me start that again. Hadzic told you Stanisic was from the DB, but through these events, as you told us yesterday, you had no idea what role the DB played, if any, in the SBWS in 1991 and 1992; is that correct? "A. Yes, it is. "Q. Looking at this paragraph again, the paragraph says: "'If he had to talk to anyone, he spoke to Goran Hadzic. I met him in Backa Palanka and in Novi Sad. I went to these places to meet Goran Hadzic but those were not official meetings with Stanisic. He just happened to be there. "Now, how do you know that if Stanisic had to talk to anyone, he spoke to Goran Hadzic? Did that come from Hadzic? "A. Yes, it did. "Q. So Goran Hadzic mentioned to you that, for example, he had gone to Belgrade and met with Stanisic, is that what he was saying at the time? "A. He didn't say that only to me, he shared it with other members of the government as well. "Q. But from what you told us, at no time did Hadzic inform you what Stanisic had said or what Stanisic had instructed or anything like that? "A. He didn't specify any instructions. He only said that he had met with Stanisic and that they had spoken. He would then convey specific instructions about how to go about solving our problems the way that would be favorable for us. "Q. But wasn't Hadzic saying that those instructions were coming from Milosevic? "A. Well, yes, for the most part he would say he had been to see Milosevic and that he had arranged with him what needs to be done and what would be the best course to take for us. It happened frequently that he said he had seen Milosevic and received instructions from him. "Mr. Jordash: Could I just take instructions, Your Honour? "Judge Orie: Please do. "Mr. Jordash: Thank you. "Q. Sorry for the delay. Mr. Bogunovic, just to pick up where we left off, is it right -- well, let me ask you in a more open way. Can you recall any instruction whatsoever from either Stanisic or anyone from the Serbian DB in relation to your work within the SBWS? "A. I cannot recall any instructions from Stanisic since I didn't know who the man was. I was introduced to him by Badza with whom I had more frequent contacts, but before meeting him in Backa Palanka and [Realtime transcript read in error "in"] Novi Sad, I had not met him before. "Q. Just so that you understand our position, Mr. Bogunovic, Mr. Stanisic had no recollection of meeting you in Backa Palanka. Are you sure that your recollection is correct? "A. I recall having met him at Ljubo Novakovic's place in Backa Palanka. I don't know how long the meeting lasted, but I do recall that particular encounter. I remember him being there. "Q. Okay. But in any event, whoever's recollection is correct, from what you recall, Stanisic didn't say anything but simply sat and took notes? "A. Yes. I don't remember him saying anything. There were several of us there and the municipal president of Backa Palanka spoke the most, as well as some people from Novi Sad, but I didn't hear Jovica Stanisic utter a single word. "Q. The meeting that you recall was focused on and concerned with the plight of refugees in the Backa Palanka region; is that correct? "A. Yes, it is. "Q. It's correct, isn't it, that you never saw Stanisic in the SBWS region in November of 1991? "A. Yes, it is correct. "Q. And you never heard that he had attended a meeting in November of 1991 involving members of the SBWS government? "A. Yes, I don't recall that. "Q. And you were never told that Stanisic attended prior to the fall of Vukovar and screamed and shouted at members of the SBWS government, berating them for failing to take Vukovar? You never heard about that; am I right? "A. No, I didn't hear that." [Interpretation] Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Bogunovic, thank you for assisting the Tribunal with your testimony. You are now released as a witness. We wish you a safe journey back home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I be excused?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I wanted just to refer to page 56 of the transcript today, lines 4 to 5. I think it said "Backa Palanka in Novi Sad," and the transcript as I was reading actually said "Backa Palanka and Novi Sad," so just to put that on the record. And finally, this is to confirm that the Prosecution is tendering the 92 package of Mr. Bogunovic of which there are only two remaining exhibits that haven't been admitted yet, but just for clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 1180 shall become Exhibit P3205.3204. And 65 ter 6066 will become Exhibit P3206.3204. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, and Your Honours, just to say that with this conclusion of this witness's evidence today, the Prosecution now rests its case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. If there is nothing else, court adjourned.
